rows.stem: Select the phase of menstrual cycle in which the remaining parts of Graafian follicle transform into the corpus luteum.
rows.solution: After ovulation, the remaining parts of the Graafian follicle transform into the **corpus luteum**. This happens in the **luteal phase**, which is also called the **secretory phase** because the corpus luteum secretes large amounts of progesterone that maintain the endometrium. The proliferative (follicular) phase comes before ovulation, and the menstrual phase is the breakdown of the endometrium. So the answer is option (A) Secretory phase.

rows.stem: A female undergoing IVF treatment has blocked fallopian tube. The technique by which the embryo with more than 8 blastomeres will be transferred into the female for further development is :
rows.solution: In IVF the ovum is fertilised outside the body and the zygote or early embryo is then transferred. An embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube (ZIFT), but an embryo with **more than 8 blastomeres** is transferred directly into the **uterus**, by **intra uterine transfer (IUT)**. Here the fallopian tube is blocked anyway, so a transfer into the tube would not help. GIFT transfers an ovum into the fallopian tube, and AI introduces semen. So the answer is option (C) IUT.

rows.stem:
Select the correct statement.
All genes located on the same chromosome :

options.label: A
options.text: form different groups depending upon their relative distance.

options.label: D
options.text: form interactive groups that affect the phenotype.

rows.solution: Genes located on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together, so they are **linked**. All the genes on one chromosome together make up **one linkage group**, and the number of linkage groups of an organism equals its haploid number of chromosomes. So the answer is option (B) form one linkage group.

rows.stem:
Choose the correct statements :
(i) Polycistronic mRNA is generally found in eukaryotes.
(ii) The RNA polymerase II transcribes precursor of mRNA, the hnRNA.
(iii) The process of translation of mRNA begins when the mRNA encounters the large subunit of ribosomes.
(iv) Stop codons do not have any tRNAs.
rows.solution:
- (i) is wrong: polycistronic mRNA is generally found in **prokaryotes**; in eukaryotes the structural genes are monocistronic.
- (ii) is correct: in eukaryotes RNA polymerase II transcribes the precursor of mRNA, the heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA).
- (iii) is wrong: translation begins when the **small subunit** of the ribosome encounters the mRNA; the large subunit joins afterwards.
- (iv) is correct: the stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA do not code for any amino acid, so no tRNA carries an anticodon for them.

So the answer is option (C) (ii) and (iv).

rows.stem: Name the extinct ancestor of humans who ate only fruits and hunted with stone weapons.
rows.solution: About 2 million years ago, the **Australopithecines** lived in the East African grasslands. Evidence shows that they hunted with stone weapons but essentially ate fruit. Ramapithecus and Dryopithecus were earlier, more ape-like primates, and Homo erectus (about 1.5 million years ago) probably ate meat. So the answer is option (B) Australopithecus.

rows.stem:
Nicotine affects blood pressure and heart rate due to release of certain adrenal hormones. Following are some of the adrenal hormones :
(i) Adrenaline
(ii) Cortisol
(iii) Noradrenaline
(iv) Aldosterone
Select the correct option :
rows.solution: Nicotine stimulates the adrenal gland to release **adrenaline** and **nor-adrenaline** into the blood circulation, and both of these raise the blood pressure and increase the heart rate. Cortisol and aldosterone are not the hormones involved. So the answer is option (D) (i) and (iii).

rows.stem: Microbes used for biocontrol of pest butterfly caterpillars is :
rows.solution: The bacterium **Bacillus thuringiensis** (Bt) is used to control butterfly caterpillars. Dried spores of Bt are mixed with water and sprayed onto vulnerable plants such as brassicas and fruit trees, where they are eaten by the insect larvae. In the gut of the larvae the toxin is released and the larvae are killed, while other insects remain unharmed. So the answer is option (B) Bacillus thuringiensis.

rows.stem:
The given diagram shows the skulls of two different mammals.
Which of the following options accurately describes the differences between these skulls ?

options.label: A
options.text: Skull B is the ancestor of skull A.

options.label: B
options.text: Skull A has more brain capacity than skull B.

options.label: C
options.text: Skull A is of a human and skull B is of an adult chimpanzee.

options.label: D
options.text: Skull A is of an adult chimpanzee and skull B is of a human.

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: two coloured drawings of skulls in side view, labelled A (left) and B (right). The shape of each skull (brain case, face, jaw) is the whole question, since every option names which skull belongs to which mammal, so it is withheld here. Page idx 8.
rows.solution: Skull A has a small, low brain case, a sloping forehead and large jaws that project forward: these are the features of an **adult chimpanzee**. Skull B has a large, rounded brain case and a flat face with small jaws: these are the features of a **human**, whose brain capacity is much larger. Neither skull is the ancestor of the other, since humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor. So the answer is option (D) Skull A is of an adult chimpanzee and skull B is of a human.

rows.stem: In RNAi, genes are silenced using which of the following biomolecules ?
rows.solution: RNA interference (RNAi) is a method of cellular defence present in all eukaryotic organisms. It silences a specific mRNA by means of a complementary **double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)** molecule, which binds to the mRNA and prevents its translation. The dsRNA may come from an infection by viruses having RNA genomes, or from mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate via an RNA intermediate. This is how nematode-resistant tobacco plants were made. So the answer is option (C) dsRNA.

rows.stem: Connell's elegant field experiments on the rocky seacoast of Scotland, found that larger barnacles Balanus dominated the intertidal area and removed the smaller barnacles Chathamalus. This happened due to :
rows.solution: In Connell's field experiments on the rocky sea coasts of Scotland, the larger and competitively superior barnacle Balanus dominated the intertidal area and excluded the smaller barnacle Chthamalus (printed here as "Chathamalus") from that zone. Both species need the same limited resource (space on the rocks), so this is interspecific **competition**, with the superior competitor excluding the inferior one. So the answer is option (D) Competition.

rows.stem: Protein encoded by gene Cry-I Ab controls the infestation of which of the following ?
rows.solution: The Bt toxin is coded by a family of genes named cry. The proteins encoded by the genes **cryIAc** and **cryIIAb** control the cotton bollworms, while the protein encoded by **cryIAb** controls the **corn borer**. So the answer is option (C) Corn borer.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Cleistogamous flowers have assured seed set.
Reason (R) : Cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous and do not depend on any pollinating agents.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: cleistogamous flowers produce assured seed set even in the absence of pollinators. The Reason is true and explains it: cleistogamous flowers do not open at all. Their anthers and stigma lie close to each other, so when the anthers dehisce, the pollen grains come in contact with the stigma of the same flower. They are therefore invariably autogamous and need no pollinating agent. So both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The human blood group 'AB' exemplifies co-dominance.
Reason (R) : The gene for human blood group trait exists in three allelic forms \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\), \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) and i.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: in a person of blood group AB, the alleles \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\) and \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) are both expressed and produce both sugars A and B on the red blood cells. This is **co-dominance**. The Reason is also true: the ABO blood group is controlled by the gene I, which has three alleles \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\), \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) and i. But having three alleles is an example of **multiple allelism**; it does not explain why \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\) and \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) are expressed together in the AB person. So both statements are true but the Reason does not explain the Assertion, which is option (B).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Nucleopolyhedrovirus are useful as they are good biocontrol agents.
Reason (R) : They are species-specific, narrow spectrum bioinsecticides.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: baculoviruses, especially those of the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus, are pathogens that attack insects and other arthropods, so they are used as biological control agents. The Reason is true and explains it: these viruses are **species-specific, narrow spectrum** insecticides. They have no negative impact on plants, mammals, birds, fish or even non-target insects, which makes them desirable in integrated pest management, especially where ecologically sensitive areas are being treated. So both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The pyramid of biomass in a pond aquatic ecosystem is always inverted.
Reason (R) : The biomass of consumers like fishes far exceeds that of the producers like phytoplanktons.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: A pyramid of biomass is inverted when the biomass of the consumers is larger than that of the producers. In water, the producers (phytoplankton) are tiny and short-lived, so at any moment their standing biomass is small even though they are reproduced rapidly, while the fishes that feed in the food chain accumulate a far larger biomass. That is why the pyramid of biomass in such water bodies is inverted, and the Reason gives exactly this cause. NCERT states this for the sea and says the pyramid is **generally** inverted, so the word "always" in the Assertion is stronger than the textbook; the board treats the Assertion as true. So both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.stem: How do 'implants' act as an effective method of contraception in human females ? Mention one advantage of implants over contraceptive pills.
rows.solution:
Implants are small capsules containing **progestogens alone or progestogen-estrogen combinations**, placed under the skin. Their mode of action is like that of the pills: they **inhibit ovulation** and implantation, and they change the quality of the cervical mucus so as to **retard the entry of sperms**.

One advantage over contraceptive pills: their effective period is **much longer**. A single implant keeps working for years, so there is no need to remember a daily pill.

rows.stem:
(a) Write one way by which apomictic seeds can be developed.
(b) Why do farmers prefer apomictic seeds over hybrid seeds ?
rows.solution:
(a) Any one way by which apomictic seeds develop:
- In some species, such as Asteraceae and grasses, the **diploid egg cell is formed without reduction division** and develops into the embryo without fertilisation.
- In many varieties of citrus and mango, some of the **nucellar cells** surrounding the embryo sac start dividing, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos.

(b) The progeny of hybrid seeds segregate, so they do not keep the hybrid characters, and the farmer must buy fresh hybrid seed every year, which is expensive. If the hybrids are made apomictic, there is **no segregation of characters** in the progeny. The farmer can then keep using the hybrid seeds to raise new crops year after year, which makes them **cost effective**.

rows.stem:
A laboratory assistant collected three water samples, namely river water, untreated sewage water and secondary effluent discharged from a sewage treatment plant. But the laboratory attendant did not note which was which. The samples were labelled A, B and C and subjected to a BOD test. The BOD values of the three samples A, B and C were recorded as 30 mg/L, 8 mg/L and 400 mg/L respectively.
(a) Which sample of the water is most polluted ?
(b) Can you assign the correct label to each, assuming the river water is relatively clean ?
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: it labels A (30 mg/L) as the river water and B (8 mg/L) as the secondary effluent. The question's own assumption that the river water is relatively clean points the other way: the lowest BOD, 8 mg/L, belongs to the relatively clean river, and secondary treatment lowers the BOD of sewage a great deal but leaves some organic matter, which fits 30 mg/L.]

BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) is the amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria. The greater the BOD, the more organic matter the water carries and the more polluted it is.

(a) Sample **C** (BOD 400 mg/L) is the most polluted, since it has the highest BOD.

(b) The labels:
- Sample C (400 mg/L): **untreated sewage water**, which carries the most organic matter.
- Sample A (30 mg/L): **secondary effluent**, whose BOD has been reduced greatly by the microbes in the aeration tanks.
- Sample B (8 mg/L): **river water**, the relatively clean sample with the lowest BOD.

rows.stem: Write the role of 'ori' and 'restriction' site in a cloning vector pBR322.
rows.solution:
- **ori**: the sequence from where replication starts. Any piece of DNA linked to this sequence can be made to replicate within the host cells, and ori also controls the **copy number** of the linked DNA.
- **Restriction site**: a recognition site for a restriction enzyme (pBR322 has sites for EcoRI, HindIII, BamHI, SalI, PstI, PvuI and ClaI), where the vector is cut so that the alien DNA can be **ligated** into it. When the alien DNA is ligated at a site inside an antibiotic resistance gene, for example the BamHI site in the tetracycline resistance gene, the plasmid loses that resistance by insertional inactivation. This lets the recombinants be selected, with the antibiotic resistance genes acting as selectable markers.

rows.stem: Biodiversity must be conserved as it plays an important role in many ecosystem services that nature provides. Explain any two ecosystem services.
rows.solution:
Any two ecosystem services provided by biodiversity:
- **Production of oxygen**: the Amazon forest alone is estimated to produce, through photosynthesis, about 20 per cent of the total oxygen in the earth's atmosphere.
- **Pollination**: without pollination plants cannot give us fruits or seeds. Nature provides this service free through pollinators such as bees, bumblebees, birds and bats.
- **Maintaining the balance of the ecosystem**: through photosynthesis, the cycling of nutrients, the generation of fertile soil, and the mitigation of droughts and floods.
- **Aesthetic, cultural and spiritual values**, and habitats for wildlife.

rows.stem:
(i) State, what does 'standing crop' of a trophic level represent.
(ii) List any two ways of measuring the standing crop of a trophic level.
rows.solution:
(i) The **standing crop** of a trophic level is the mass of living material (biomass) present at that trophic level at a particular time.

(ii) It is measured as:
- the **biomass** of the living organisms, as dry weight per unit area; or
- the **number** of organisms per unit area.

rows.stem: Differentiate between wind-pollinated and insect-pollinated flowers. Give an example of each type.
rows.solution:
Any four differences:

| Wind-pollinated flowers | Insect-pollinated flowers |
|---|---|
| Flowers are small, dull and not colourful | Flowers are large and colourful |
| No nectar and no fragrance | Usually produce nectar and are fragrant |
| Pollen grains produced in very large numbers | Pollen grains produced in smaller numbers |
| Pollen grains light, dry and non-sticky | Pollen grains heavy and sticky |
| Stigma large and often feathery, to trap pollen carried in the air | Stigma not feathery, often sticky |
| Well-exposed stamens | Stamens usually enclosed within the flower |

Examples: wind-pollinated, **maize** or other grasses; insect-pollinated, **sunflower** or Salvia.

rows.stem:
(a) Construct a complete transcription unit with promoter and terminator on the basis of the hypothetical coding strand given below :
A T G C A T G C A T A G
(b) Write the RNA strand transcribed from the above transcription unit along with its polarity.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE: the twelve bases A T G C A T G C A T A G printed above a horizontal line with a tick under each base and an arrowhead at BOTH ends. No 5' or 3' end is marked anywhere, which is why the scheme accepts either polarity. The bases are carried in the stem. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
(a) A transcription unit has three regions: a **promoter**, the **structural gene** and a **terminator**. Taking the printed coding strand as running 5' to 3' from left to right:
- coding strand: 5'-ATGCATGCATAG-3'
- template strand: 3'-TACGTACGTATC-5'

The **promoter** is located towards the **5' end (upstream)** of the coding strand, at the left of the drawn strand, and provides the binding site for RNA polymerase. The **terminator** is located towards the **3' end (downstream)** of the coding strand, at the right, and defines the end of transcription. Each strand is labelled with its 5' and 3' ends, and the two strands are labelled coding strand and template strand.

(b) The RNA is transcribed on the template strand (3' to 5'), so it has the same sequence as the coding strand with uracil in place of thymine:

5'-AUGCAUGCAUAG-3'

The printed strand marks no polarity, so the marking scheme also accepts the opposite reading: the coding strand taken as 3'-ATGCATGCATAG-5' from left to right, with the promoter on the right, which gives the RNA 5'-GAUACGUACGUA-3'.

rows.stem: Explain the three different ways in which natural selection operates. Explain with the help of graphs.
rows.solution:
Natural selection can operate in three ways on a character, such as height, that shows a normal distribution in a population. Each is drawn as a graph of the number of individuals against the value of the character.
- **Stabilising selection**: more individuals acquire the mean character value, so variation is much reduced. The graph: the peak stays at the mean but gets **higher and narrower**.
- **Directional selection**: more individuals acquire a value other than the mean character value. The graph: the **peak shifts in one direction**.
- **Disruptive selection**: more individuals acquire the peripheral character values at both ends of the distribution curve. The graph: **two peaks** form, one at each end, with a dip at the mean.

rows.stem:
(a) How do some viruses cause cancer in humans ?
(b) How do benign tumours turn malignant ? How do malignant tumours harm the human body ?
rows.solution:
(a) Some viruses, called **oncogenic viruses**, have genes called **viral oncogenes**. When such a virus infects a human cell, these genes transform the normal cell into a cancerous cell, which divides in an uncontrolled way.

(b) A benign tumour normally remains confined to its original location. It turns malignant when its cells acquire the property of **metastasis**: cells slough off from the tumour, reach distant sites through the blood, and wherever they lodge they start a new tumour.

Malignant tumours harm the body because they are a mass of proliferating neoplastic cells that grow very rapidly, **invade and damage the surrounding normal tissues**, and **compete with the normal cells for vital nutrients**, starving them.

rows.stem:
(a) How is insulin different from proinsulin ?
(b) Explain all the stages of how human insulin is produced through rDNA technology.
rows.solution:
(a) Insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains, chain A and chain B, linked together by disulphide bridges. Proinsulin is the prohormone in which it is first synthesised: it contains an **extra stretch called the C-peptide** in addition to chains A and B. The C-peptide is removed during maturation, so it is **not present in mature insulin**.

(b) The stages of producing human insulin by rDNA technology:
- In 1983, Eli Lilly, an American company, prepared **two DNA sequences** corresponding to the **A and B chains** of human insulin.
- These were introduced into **plasmids of E. coli**, which produced the insulin chains.
- Chains A and B were produced separately, **extracted** and purified.
- They were then **combined by creating disulphide bonds** to form human insulin.

rows.stem:
Study the graph given below and answer the questions that follow :
(i) Write the status of food and space in the curves a and b.
(ii) In the absence of predators, which one of the two curves would appropriately depict the prey population ?
(iii) 'Time' has been shown on x-axis and there is a parallel dotted line above it. Give the significance of this dotted line.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a graph of Population density (N) on the y-axis against Time (t) on the x-axis, with two curves labelled a and b rising from the origin and a horizontal dashed line drawn across the upper part of the graph. Which curve keeps rising past the dashed line and which levels off at it decides (i) and (ii), so the shapes are withheld here. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
(i) Curve a is J-shaped (exponential growth): the **food and space are unlimited**. Curve b is S-shaped or sigmoid (logistic growth): the **food and space are limited**, so growth slows and levels off.

(ii) **Curve a**. In the absence of predators the prey population is not checked, so it grows exponentially.

(iii) The dotted line represents the **carrying capacity (K)**: the maximum number of individuals that a given environment can support, beyond which further growth of the population is not possible.

rows.stem:
Answer the following questions :
(i) Define 'predation'.
(ii) Why is predation required in a community of different organisms ? Give any two points.
(iii) Why are predators 'prudent' in nature ?
rows.solution:
(i) **Predation** is an interspecific interaction in which one animal, the predator, kills and consumes another animal, the prey.

(ii) Any two reasons why predation is required in a community:
- Predators keep the **prey populations under control**.
- They help in **maintaining species diversity** in a community by reducing the intensity of competition among competing prey species.
- Predators act as **conduits for energy transfer** across trophic levels.
- Biological control methods in agricultural pest control are based on the ability of the predator to regulate the prey population.

(iii) Predators are said to be 'prudent' because they do not over-exploit their prey. If a predator were too efficient and over-exploited its prey, the prey might become extinct, and following it the predator would also become extinct for lack of food.

rows.stem:
There are many animals, which have become extinct in the wild, but continue to be maintained in zoological parks. Answer the questions that follow :
(a) What type of bio-diversity conservation is observed in this case ?
(b) Explain any other two ways which help in this type of conservation.
(c) Besides zoological parks, mention one place that serves this purpose.
rows.solution:
(a) This is **ex situ conservation**: threatened animals are taken out of their natural habitat and protected in special settings.

(b) Any two other ways that help ex situ conservation:
- **Cryopreservation**: the gametes (sperms or eggs) or embryos of threatened species can be preserved in viable and fertile condition for long periods at \(-196^\circ\text{C}\), in liquid nitrogen.
- **In vitro fertilisation and tissue culture**: eggs can be fertilised in vitro, and plants can be propagated using tissue culture methods.
- **Seed banks**: seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants can be kept for long periods.

(c) **Wildlife safari parks**. (Botanical gardens serve the same purpose for plants.)

rows.stem: It is said that 'lac operon' has to be operational at a very low level in the bacterial cell all the time. Justify.
rows.context: Gene expresses itself in a cell system as a protein/enzyme. How an expression of gene occurs in a cell system, when it needs to occur and how the gene expression is regulated in prokaryotic cell system was studied by the combined efforts of Francois Jacob, a geneticist and Jacques Monod, a biochemist. For their work on lactose metabolism in E. coli and introducing the concept of 'lac operon', they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1965.
rows.solution: The enzyme permease, coded by the y gene of the lac operon, increases the permeability of the cell to lactose. If the operon were completely switched off, there would be no permease in the cell, lactose could **not enter the cell**, and so it could never act as the inducer to switch the operon on. A very low level of expression of the lac operon must therefore be present in the cell all the time.

rows.stem: How are the structural genes activated in the lac operon in E. coli ?
rows.context: Gene expresses itself in a cell system as a protein/enzyme. How an expression of gene occurs in a cell system, when it needs to occur and how the gene expression is regulated in prokaryotic cell system was studied by the combined efforts of Francois Jacob, a geneticist and Jacques Monod, a biochemist. For their work on lactose metabolism in E. coli and introducing the concept of 'lac operon', they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1965.
rows.solution: The repressor of the operon is synthesised all the time from the i gene. In the presence of the inducer, lactose (or allolactose), the repressor is **inactivated by its interaction with the inducer** and cannot bind to the operator. This allows **RNA polymerase access to the promoter**, and transcription of the structural genes z, y and a proceeds.

rows.stem: Why is the regulation of operon called negative regulation ?
rows.context: Gene expresses itself in a cell system as a protein/enzyme. How an expression of gene occurs in a cell system, when it needs to occur and how the gene expression is regulated in prokaryotic cell system was studied by the combined efforts of Francois Jacob, a geneticist and Jacques Monod, a biochemist. For their work on lactose metabolism in E. coli and introducing the concept of 'lac operon', they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1965.
rows.solution: The regulation of the lac operon by the repressor is called **negative regulation** because the operon is kept **switched off**: in the absence of the inducer, the repressor binds to the operator and prevents transcription. The operon is expressed only when the inducer removes this block.

rows.stem: Why is lac operon said to be a transcriptionally regulated system ?
rows.context: Gene expresses itself in a cell system as a protein/enzyme. How an expression of gene occurs in a cell system, when it needs to occur and how the gene expression is regulated in prokaryotic cell system was studied by the combined efforts of Francois Jacob, a geneticist and Jacques Monod, a biochemist. For their work on lactose metabolism in E. coli and introducing the concept of 'lac operon', they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1965.
rows.solution:
The lac operon is regulated at the level of **initiation of transcription**:
- In the absence of the inducer, the repressor binds to the operator and **prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing** the structural genes.
- When the inducer (lactose) is present, it prevents the repressor from binding to the operator, and transcription of the structural genes takes place.

Since whether the genes are expressed is decided by whether they are transcribed, it is a transcriptionally regulated system.

rows.stem: Name the two types of specialised cells which carry out the primary and secondary responses.
rows.context: Immunity in our body is of two types (i) Innate immunity, and (ii) Acquired immunity. Innate immunity is a non-specific defence mechanism, whereas Acquired immunity is pathogen specific. Acquired immunity is characterised by memory. Antibodies are specific to antigens and there are four types of antibodies produced in our body — IgA, IgE, IgG and IgM. It shows primary response where it encounters the pathogen for the first time and secondary response during the subsequent encounters with the same antigen/pathogen. These immune responses are carried out with the help of two special types of lymphocytes present in the blood.
rows.solution: The two special types of lymphocytes are the **B-lymphocytes** (B cells) and the **T-lymphocytes** (T cells).

rows.stem: Name any two barriers present in our body that provide innate immunity.
rows.context: Immunity in our body is of two types (i) Innate immunity, and (ii) Acquired immunity. Innate immunity is a non-specific defence mechanism, whereas Acquired immunity is pathogen specific. Acquired immunity is characterised by memory. Antibodies are specific to antigens and there are four types of antibodies produced in our body — IgA, IgE, IgG and IgM. It shows primary response where it encounters the pathogen for the first time and secondary response during the subsequent encounters with the same antigen/pathogen. These immune responses are carried out with the help of two special types of lymphocytes present in the blood.
rows.solution:
Any two of the barriers of innate immunity:
- **Physical barriers**: the skin, and the mucus coating of the epithelium lining the respiratory, gastro-intestinal and urogenital tracts.
- **Physiological barriers**: acid in the stomach, saliva in the mouth, and tears from the eyes.
- **Cellular barriers**: leukocytes such as PMNL-neutrophils and monocytes, natural killer cells, and macrophages.
- **Cytokine barriers**: interferons secreted by virus-infected cells, which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection.

rows.stem: The organ transplants (grafts) are often rejected if not taken from suitable compatible persons. Mention the characteristic of our immune system that is responsible for the rejection.
rows.context: Immunity in our body is of two types (i) Innate immunity, and (ii) Acquired immunity. Innate immunity is a non-specific defence mechanism, whereas Acquired immunity is pathogen specific. Acquired immunity is characterised by memory. Antibodies are specific to antigens and there are four types of antibodies produced in our body — IgA, IgE, IgG and IgM. It shows primary response where it encounters the pathogen for the first time and secondary response during the subsequent encounters with the same antigen/pathogen. These immune responses are carried out with the help of two special types of lymphocytes present in the blood.
rows.solution: The immune system has the ability to **differentiate between 'self' and 'non-self'** cells and tissues. A graft from an incompatible person is recognised as non-self, and the **cell-mediated immune response**, carried out by the T-lymphocytes, rejects it.

rows.stem: How is active immunity different from passive immunity ? Write any two differences.
rows.context: Immunity in our body is of two types (i) Innate immunity, and (ii) Acquired immunity. Innate immunity is a non-specific defence mechanism, whereas Acquired immunity is pathogen specific. Acquired immunity is characterised by memory. Antibodies are specific to antigens and there are four types of antibodies produced in our body — IgA, IgE, IgG and IgM. It shows primary response where it encounters the pathogen for the first time and secondary response during the subsequent encounters with the same antigen/pathogen. These immune responses are carried out with the help of two special types of lymphocytes present in the blood.
rows.solution:
Any two differences:

| Active immunity | Passive immunity |
|---|---|
| Antibodies are produced by the body itself in response to an antigen | Ready-made (preformed) antibodies are given to the body for protection |
| Slow: takes time to give its full effective response | Quick: gives an immediate response |
| Long lasting | Lasts for a shorter period |
| Memory cells are formed | Memory cells are not formed |

rows.stem:
Study the flow chart given below. Name the hormones involved at each stage and explain their functions.
Hypothalamus
\(\downarrow\)
Pituitary
\(\downarrow\)
Ovary
\(\downarrow\)
Pregnancy
rows.solution:
The hormones at each stage and their functions:
- **Hypothalamus**: secretes **gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH)**, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release the gonadotropins FSH and LH, both of which act on the ovary.
- **Pituitary**: secretes **follicle stimulating hormone (FSH)**, which stimulates the development of the follicles and the secretion of estrogen by the follicle cells.
- **Pituitary**: also secretes **luteinising hormone (LH)**. A rapid rise of LH in the middle of the cycle (the LH surge) induces ovulation, and LH stimulates the formation of the corpus luteum from the ruptured Graafian follicle.
- **Ovary**: the growing follicles secrete **estrogen**, which brings about the maturation of the primary follicle into the Graafian follicle and the regeneration of the endometrium.
- **Ovary**: the corpus luteum secretes **progesterone**, which maintains the endometrium. This is necessary for the implantation of the fertilised ovum and for the other events of pregnancy.

rows.stem:

Write the types and locations of the genes causing thalassemia in humans. State the cause and symptoms of the disease. How is sickle-cell anemia different from this disease ?
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: its second difference says that in thalassemia "both \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) chain are affected". A given thalassemia reduces one kind of chain, the \(\alpha\) chain in \(\alpha\) thalassemia or the \(\beta\) chain in \(\beta\) thalassemia. The contrast intended is that thalassemia can involve either chain, while sickle-cell anaemia involves only the \(\beta\) chain.]

**Types and locations of the genes:**
- **\(\alpha\) thalassemia** is controlled by two closely linked genes, **HBA1 and HBA2**, both on **chromosome 16**.
- **\(\beta\) thalassemia** is controlled by a single gene, **HBB**, on **chromosome 11**.

**Cause:** thalassemia is an autosomal recessive blood disease transmitted from parents who are both unaffected carriers. It is due to the **mutation or deletion** of one or more of the alleles of these genes (four alleles in \(\alpha\) thalassemia, two in \(\beta\) thalassemia). This reduces the rate of synthesis of one of the globin chains, so abnormal haemoglobin molecules are formed.

**Symptoms:** anaemia, extreme tiredness, pale skin and breathlessness.

**Difference from sickle-cell anaemia:** thalassemia is a **quantitative** problem, in which too few globin molecules are synthesised. Sickle-cell anaemia is a **qualitative** problem, in which an incorrectly functioning globin is synthesised: a single substitution of valine for glutamic acid at the sixth position of the \(\beta\) chain makes the red blood cells sickle-shaped under low oxygen tension.

rows.stem:
(i) Enlist any four prime goals of the Human Genome Project (HGP).
(ii) List the two methodologies which were involved in the human genome project. Mention how they were used.
(iii) Expand 'YAC' and mention what it was used for.
rows.solution:
(i) Any four goals of the Human Genome Project:
- Identify all the approximately **20,000-25,000 genes** in human DNA.
- Determine the **sequences of the 3 billion chemical base pairs** that make up human DNA.
- **Store this information** in databases.
- **Improve tools for data analysis**.
- **Transfer related technologies** to other sectors, such as industries.
- Address the **ethical, legal and social issues** that may arise from the project.

(ii) The two methodologies:
- **Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs)**: identifying all the genes that are expressed as RNA.
- **Sequence annotation**: sequencing the whole set of the genome, all the coding and non-coding sequences, and later assigning functions to the different regions of the sequence.

For sequencing, the total DNA of a cell was isolated, broken into random fragments of small size, cloned in a suitable host using special vectors and amplified, and the fragments were sequenced with automated DNA sequencers. Computer programs then arranged the overlapping fragments into the full sequence.

(iii) YAC stands for **Yeast Artificial Chromosome**. It was used as a **vector** to clone the large fragments of human DNA in a host so that they could be amplified and sequenced (bacterial artificial chromosomes, BAC, were used in the same way).

rows.stem:
(i) EcoR I has played a very important role in rDNA technology.
(I) Explain the convention for naming EcoR I.
(II) Write the recognition site of this endonuclease restriction enzyme.
(ii) Name the overhanging stretches of DNA produced by these restriction enzymes. Describe their role in the formation of rDNA.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: it says the first letter E comes from the "genes" (Escherichia); it comes from the genus.]

(i) (I) The naming convention for EcoRI:
- the first letter, **E**, comes from the **genus**, Escherichia;
- the next two letters, **co**, come from the **species**, coli;
- the letter **R** comes from the name of the **strain** (RY 13);
- the Roman numeral **I** indicates the **order** in which the enzyme was isolated from that strain of the bacterium.

(II) EcoRI recognises the palindromic sequence

5'-GAATTC-3'
3'-CTTAAG-5'

and cuts each strand between G and A.

(ii) The overhanging stretches are called **sticky ends**. They are called so because they form **hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts**. When the vector DNA and the source DNA are cut with the same restriction enzyme, both carry the same kind of sticky ends, so the pieces pair up. This stickiness facilitates the action of the enzyme **DNA ligase**, which joins the ends and so forms the recombinant DNA.

rows.stem:
(i) Insertional inactivation is a method to detect the recombinant DNA. Explain this method.
(ii) Name the commonly used vector for transferring genes in plants from bacteria.
(iii) How is this able to transform a normal plant cell into a tumour ?
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: its answer to (iii) says the bacterium delivers "T-DNA or Ti tumor-inducing plasmid" into the plant cell. Only the T-DNA, a segment of the Ti plasmid, is transferred; the plasmid itself stays in the bacterium.]

(i) In **insertional inactivation**, the alien DNA is inserted within the coding sequence of the enzyme **\(\beta\)-galactosidase** in the vector. This inactivates the enzyme.
- The bacteria are grown on a medium containing a **chromogenic substrate**. Colonies whose plasmid has **no insert** (non-recombinants) make active \(\beta\)-galactosidase and give **blue coloured colonies**.
- Colonies that **do not produce any colour** are identified as **recombinants**, because their gene for the enzyme has been inactivated by the insert.

(ii) **Agrobacterium tumefaciens**, a pathogen of several dicot plants (its Ti plasmid is used as the vector).

(iii) Agrobacterium tumefaciens delivers a piece of DNA known as **T-DNA**, part of its tumour inducing (Ti) plasmid, into the plant cell. The T-DNA transforms the normal plant cell into a **tumour** cell and directs the tumour cells to produce the chemicals the pathogen requires.
